MAN: It starts around 6:00pm downtown, and it takes about two hours for it to travel the full distance. Spring Garden Road is the best place to watch because that's halfway on the route, and you're close to shops and restaurants.
WOMAN: That sounds good, and the parade probably finishes there in an hour. I guess we need lots of time beforehand to find parking, though. It's going to be busy, right?

MAN: Hey Anika, you're home early today! Do you have a minute? I was hoping you could look at my resumé. I've used it to apply for tons of jobs, but I haven't gotten a single response! I could really use your expert opinion.
WOMAN: (laughing) Well, "expert opinion" might be an exaggeration-I'm no professional. But, I have helped quite a few people in the past... [pause] Okay, so, taking a quick look, you don't seem to be showing your strengths with this resumé.
MAN: That makes sense. I know I have the qualifications, but it's been a long time since I've had to do a resumé.
WOMAN: Well, my first suggestion is to make your resumé stand out in some way. It may seem simple, but some colour and an interesting font can be eye-catching and entice someone to actually take a look at your resumé. You'll also need to do more than just list your past jobs.
MAN: That's a great idea! I didn't even think of colour and appearance… For content I thought the whole point was to list the jobs I've held over the last 10 years, with a few details about my roles and responsibilities.
WOMAN: Well, these days employers often hire people who can show the impact they've made in their companies. Since you want to highlight your leadership experience, you should definitely mention the sales and marketing seminars you conducted. Those boosted profits for your previous company 3 years in a row, right? That's a big deal!
MAN: Yes, good point! I hadn't thought of that. Any other advice?
WOMAN: Well, you may want to rearrange your resumé a bit because it's very chronological. Although it's good to have an overview of what you've done over the years, you should briefly mention your professional skills first.
MAN: Do you mean things like project management, budgeting, and business negotiation?
WOMAN: Yes, exactly! Not everyone possesses those skills, so you really should put them at the top of your resumé.
MAN: These are really useful suggestions! Thanks so much! I'm so glad I asked you.
WOMAN: Great! Just a few minor fixes and you'll be getting those phone calls you've been hoping for! Oh, before you go-just let me run inside the house and grab the book you lent me. It was a great read!

A local man went home happy after collecting an award at the city's annual Houseplant Show, held at the downtown Rhodes Arena this past weekend. Justin Wilson, 53, set a new record for the tallest cactus ever grown indoors.
When asked how he managed to grow the 3.5-metre beast, he claimed it was nothing but good fortune. Wilson accepted the award for his oddity from Michael Cole, head organizer of the event and an ecologist at Maplewood University. Cole says that he sees cacti as tall as Wilson's all the time in the desert, but never in someone's home.

Eric: Thanks for coming today. So, Fall Soccer is just around the corner and we want to make sure online registration goes smoothly. We had a lot of glitches last year-and complaints.
Ian: Oh, I remember that. [groaning] I spent hours fixing those issues and calming frenzied parents. I just overhauled the registration section on our website, so I don't anticipate the same problems this year.
Alyssa: I'm glad you were the one dealing with that. You're the techie! [slight pause] On another note, we've had a lot of inquiries about our fees. Can we manage to keep them the same as last year?
Eric: Good question. We're looking at a 5% increase. But we need to stick to our mandate - developing players in the local community. I don't want cost to become an obstacle. Families are already paying for registration, photography, uniforms, shoes, snacks. ..
Ian: Yeah, I'm worried that some kids won't be able to participate if it strains their family budget.
Alyssa: Yeah, with three players in my house, soccer costs add up to a small fortune!
Eric: Well, some other clubs offer discounts to parents who volunteer throughout the season. Especially the parents who help out as assistant coaches, they really offset some of the costs. What do you think?
Ian: I don't know about that. We're fortunate to have enough time to volunteer for this club, but not all parents do. What about a family discount plan? For example, full price for the first child, then ten percent off for the second. And 15 percent off for the third, in families like Alyssa's.
Alyssa: For me personally, that would be great - but it wouldn't help most of our soccer families at all. [pause] How about a 'used gear exchange'? Kids outgrow their stuff so quickly. If we set something up on our website, then parents could browse through used items when doing their registration.
Eric: That sounds good. We could add a discussion forum to our website where parents and players can arrange to buy, sell and trade their gear.
Ian: I'm not so sure about that idea. [not agreeable] From a technical perspective, it's actually more complicated than it sounds.
Alyssa: Well, we could also consider a partnership with a local sports store in the area. For example, players could show their club ID cards to get a markdown on shoes and other gear.
Eric: I can look into something like that, but in the meantime, Ian, it would be great if you could research ways to get the online forum going.

sections.transcript:
Welcome parents and staff of Cederbrook Elementary. I appreciate all of you being here tonight. It is standard practice at our school, indeed, at most schools everywhere, to issue daily homework assignments. Beginning in kindergarten, students are assigned tasks that typically take about 15 minutes to complete. With each grade level, the complexity and quantity of the assignments increases, to a maximum of about 2 hours per night for our grade eight students. Recently, this practice has been called into question.
Spearheading this debate is parent and child psychologist Jaime Lee. According to Lee, numerous studies have pointed to the detrimental impacts of daily homework. Indeed, increasingly in her practice, she is seeing these impacts. Many of her younger clients are experiencing high levels of stress, poor physical health, and feelings of isolation, with the long hours of homework after long days at school being the primary cause. According to Lee, these results are not surprising when you consider what children are giving up in order to manage their daily workloads; time with family, time with friends, time for themselves. For Lee, a child's time after school should be unstructured. She contends daily homework leads to an overemphasis on academics that fails to address all of the developmental needs of children.
Arnold Blake, president of Cederbrook Elementary's parent council, disagrees. For Blake, homework time is quality time with his child. In fact, sitting with his daughter while she does her homework is one of their favourite times of day. He appreciates knowing what his daughter is learning at school, what interests her, and what she finds challenging. Additionally, Blake believes this one-on-one attention, in the comfort of her own home, is crucial to his daughter's learning. While, initially, his daughter struggled at school, her academic performance has gotten much better since Blake became more involved. He believes that her daily assignments have played a large role in this change. While Blake acknowledges a balance must be maintained, he does not feel his daughter's development has been adversely impacted. In contrast, he has seen an increase in her confidence, a fact which has benefited all aspects of her life. In consideration of both perspectives, perhaps something we need to consider is the frame of mind of parents and children. If both the parent and child feel positive about the task, I believe homework can be a great way to improve grades and involve parents in their child's learning. However, if either party feels negative, a fifteen-minute assignment can easily turn into a two-hour disciplinary nightmare. This would clearly be counterproductive. I'll now open the floor for discussion.

paragraphs: Dear Principal Chaudry,

I am writing because I need to withdraw my son, Adam, from the Berry Hill Preschool program. I am requesting a refund of the tuition we prepaid for the period of January to June of next year.We have been very happy with Berry Hill, and Adam has been enjoying his time there. However, we find that living in Vancouver is financially difficult for our family. I have been unable to get permanent work as a teacher for almost 2 years, and I have been looking for employment in other cities which can offer a more stable situation for us. Last week, I accepted a position teaching grade 10 at a high school in Calgary, and we will move in December.

My wife and I knew that when we enrolled Adam in the school we would be responsible for paying a full year of tuition, but I respectfully ask that you make an exception in our case due to our circumstances. We will be moving away, and there is simply no way we can afford to pay for our move plus make payments for a school Adam is not even attending.

I understand that we still need to forfeit the $400 deposit we made when we initially signed the contract, and that is all right with us. However, I must ask you to consider allowing us to cancel the contract due to our move to Calgary.

Unfortunately, even if Berry Hill is unable to release us from the contract, I will still ask the bank to cancel the post-dated cheques we gave you in September, simply because it does not make sense for us to pay.
Dear Principal Chaudry,

I hope you understand the difficult situation we are in. Again, I want to tell you that we have had a very positive experience with your school. Because he's so shy, it took Adam a while to get comfortable with everyone at the school, but now he is enjoying the friendly, stimulating environment.
Thank you for your time and understanding.
Sincerely,
Bart Wang

paragraphs: A. Caribana is an annual summer arts and culture carnival held in Toronto, Ontario. It's modelled after many such carnivals occurring throughout the Caribbean islands and is now the largest festival of its kind in North America. Every year Caribana draws more than two million people, many of whom come to Canada just for the impressively elaborate event. Thanks to Caribana, about $400 million a year flows into Ontario, about half of which goes to the government in tax revenues.

B. Caribana-the name is intended to suggest both the Caribbean and Canada-started in 1967 as the Caribbean community's contribution to Canada's centennial celebrations. It celebrates not only Canada's centennial, but also Caribbean culture and the African emancipation, when the enslavement of African people in Canada was declared illegal on August 1, 1834. However, since the 1980s, Caribana has included elaborate and impressive contributions from cultural groups in Central America, South America, and Africa, as well.

C. The festival celebrates music with indigenous songs and instrumental music including calypso, soca, reggae, and salsa. The performers' contributions include not only music but also dance, masquerade, and oral traditions that feature storytellers and comedians performing in "talk tents." Arguably the most significant events in the two-week festival are the steel band street parties. The steel drum, originating from Trinidad and Tobago, is the only non-electric musical instrument invented in the twentieth century. In fact, one notable moment from the first Caribana was a flawless three-piece performance by a steel band during a blackout caused by a rainstorm. In addition to all the entertainment, visitors may indulge in a variety of Caribbean food ranging from the expensive to the economical.

D. The highlight of the festival, however, is the grand parade. Although its route has changed over the years, it continues to be an electrifying spectacle of colour, costumes, music, and dance that covers several miles, dazzling the dense crowds that line both sides of the streets. However, since this parade is carnival style, anyone can join in and contribute in their own way. Parade participants are organized into masquerade groups called "bands" (now over a hundred), each of which has a particular theme-historical, political, fantastical-and is led by a "king" or "queen." The parade is also a competition, and the bands are judged on elements including energy, creativity, and costumes that are typically quite lavish.
E. Not given in any of the above paragraphs.

paragraphs: Ever heard of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, or Verrucomicrobia? While these names might sound like an alien species from a thriller movie, they are, in fact, microscopic residents within our very own bodies. Indeed, they're just a few of the many microorganisms which make up the human microbiome, a term which refers to all of the microorganisms within the human body. It turns out that a healthy human body is teeming with a wide variety of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and even viruses, with many human ailments linked to a reduction in this diversity.

According to researcher Ellie Kim, her investigations have found correlations between human microbiomes and a diverse array of diseases. "The role that these tiny creatures appear to have on health is profound and will open doors to new kinds of medical treatments," Kim enthuses. She envisions that correcting microbiome imbalances may soon replace the practice of wiping out entire colonies of microorganisms with antibiotics. Indeed, with antibiotic-resistant bacteria on the rise, our current methods of treating bacterial illnesses are becoming worryingly obsolete.

Dietician Carlos Gomez is unconvinced. He contends that it isn't clear whether the microbiome changes associated with various diseases are the cause of, or simply the secondary effect, of disease. "Studies have found both a decrease in gut diversity and a rise in gastrointestinal illnesses when travellers eat new dishes," says Gomez. He acknowledges that gut microorganisms typically undergo changes when digesting unfamiliar foods. Gomez emphasizes, "It's uncertain whether supplementing yourself with a better balance of microorganisms, without an accompanying avoidance of these foods, would impact overall gut health."

Magali Beauchamp, however, is willing to take her chances. Although stomach troubles aren't a concern for her, Beauchamp struggled with eczema-a skin condition-for years. She tried an array of the usual topical treatments, but to no avail. Under her doctor's supervision, she resorted to probiotics, which are live microorganisms which can be consumed to balance the body's microbiome. Within months, she found relief. A now healthy Beauchamp markets probiotic foods to stores across Canada, believing everyone can benefit from a few extra critters.

tasks.title: Writing an Email
scenario: You live across from an elementary school where a construction team is working outside. You notice that the construction site does not have a safety fence around it and that it is too noisy during class. You are worried about children getting hurt after school or having difficulty learning in class.
tasks.instruction: Write an email to the construction company in about 150-200 words. Your email should do the following things:
bullets: Suggest how they could work more safely

paragraphs: I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to express my concerns regarding the construction site located across from the elementary school. As a resident in the neighborhood, I have observed several safety issues that need immediate attention.

Firstly, I noticed that the construction site lacks a proper safety fence. This poses a significant risk to the children who play in the area after school. Without a barrier, they could easily wander into the site and get injured by heavy machinery or construction materials. Additionally, the noise levels during school hours are excessively high, which could disrupt the students' ability to concentrate and learn effectively.

To address these issues, I suggest installing a sturdy safety fence around the perimeter of the construction site to prevent unauthorized access. Furthermore, implementing noise reduction measures, such as using quieter equipment or scheduling noisier activities outside of school hours, would greatly benefit the students and teachers.
Thank you for your attention to this matter. I trust that you will take the necessary steps to ensure the safety and well-being of our community.
Regards,
[Name]

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the ongoing construction project near the elementary school. As a resident living directly across from the school, I have observed several safety issues that require immediate attention.

Firstly, I have noticed the absence of a safety fence around the construction site. This poses a significant risk to the children, especially during after-school hours when they might wander into the area. Additionally, the noise levels during class hours are excessively high, making it difficult for students to concentrate on their studies. The constant drilling and machinery sounds are disruptive to the learning environment.

tasks.title: Responding to Survey Questions
scenario: The city council is considering two empty sites as possible places to build a new airport. All residents are being asked to complete an opinion survey. One is in the downtown area and the other is 10 km away from the city centre.
tasks.instruction: Choose the option that you prefer. Why do you prefer your choice? Explain the reasons for your choice. Write about 150-200 words.
options: Option A: I think the airport should be built in the downtown area.
Option B: I think the airport should be built far from the downtown area.

paragraphs: I strongly believe that the new airport should be constructed 10 kilometers away from the downtown area. This location offers significant advantages for both the city's development and residents' quality of life.

Firstly, building the airport outside the city center would minimize noise pollution and traffic congestion in the downtown area. The constant noise from aircraft taking off and landing would significantly disrupt businesses, schools, and residential areas if the airport were located downtown. Additionally, the increased traffic from airport operations would exacerbate existing transportation challenges in the city center.

Secondly, the remote location provides ample space for future expansion and development. Unlike the limited space available downtown, the suburban site can accommodate larger runways, additional terminals, and supporting infrastructure without space constraints. This forward-thinking approach ensures the airport can meet growing demand and adapt to future technological advancements in aviation.

In conclusion, while the downtown location might offer some convenience, the long-term benefits of the suburban site far outweigh this advantage. The remote location better serves the city's sustainable development goals and protects residents' quality of life.

I firmly believe that the new airport should be constructed in the downtown area rather than 10 kilometers away from the city center. This decision is based on two compelling reasons: accessibility and economic benefits.

Firstly, a downtown airport would provide unparalleled convenience for both residents and visitors. The central location would significantly reduce travel time for the majority of users, particularly business travelers who often have tight schedules. This accessibility would also benefit tourists, making our city more attractive as a destination. Furthermore, the integration with existing public transportation systems would be more efficient, reducing traffic congestion and environmental impact.

Secondly, the economic advantages of a downtown airport are substantial. The construction and operation of the airport would create numerous job opportunities in the heart of the city. Additionally, the increased foot traffic would stimulate local businesses, from hotels to restaurants, contributing to the overall economic growth of the downtown area. This development could potentially transform our city center into a vibrant hub of activity.

In conclusion, while both locations have their merits, the downtown area offers superior accessibility and economic potential. I strongly recommend that the city council consider these factors when making their final decision.
I strongly believe that the new airport should be constructed 10 km away from the downtown area. This decision is based on two crucial factors: environmental impact and urban development.

Firstly, building an airport in the downtown area would significantly increase noise and air pollution, negatively affecting the quality of life for residents. The constant noise from aircraft would disrupt daily activities, while increased air traffic would worsen air quality. In contrast, a location outside the city center would minimize these impacts, preserving the downtown's livability.

Secondly, constructing the airport away from the city center would promote balanced urban growth. It would encourage the development of new residential and commercial areas around the airport, creating job opportunities and stimulating economic growth in less developed regions. This approach would prevent overconcentration of infrastructure in the downtown area, which is already facing space constraints.
In conclusion, while both locations have their merits, the site 10 km from downtown offers a more sustainable solution that benefits both the environment and the city's long-term development.

In conclusion, while building the airport downtown might seem convenient initially, the long-term benefits of a remote location far outweigh the temporary advantages. The 10 km site would create a more sustainable and efficient transportation hub for our city's future.

tasks.title: Giving Advice
prompt: Your friend started a new job and is a very shy person. She would like to get to know her co-workers. Advise her about different ways to make friends at work.

paragraphs: Hey there, I totally get that starting a new job can be nerve-wracking, especially if you're shy. But don't worry, I've got some tips that might help you break the ice with your co-workers.

First off, try joining in on group activities or social events at work. Whether it's a lunch outing or a team-building exercise, these are great opportunities to chat in a more relaxed setting. For example, you could suggest grabbing coffee together during a break - it's a simple way to start a conversation.

Another thing you could do is ask for help or advice on work-related tasks. People generally enjoy sharing their expertise, and it's a natural way to build rapport. You might say something like, 'Hey, I'm new to this project - do you have any tips on how to approach it?'

One final thing is to show genuine interest in your co-workers' lives. Ask about their weekend plans or hobbies. People love talking about themselves, and it can lead to discovering common interests. For instance, if someone mentions they enjoy hiking, you could share your own experiences or ask for trail recommendations.

Remember, making friends takes time, so be patient with yourself. Most people are more approachable than they seem, and your co-workers will likely appreciate your efforts to connect. Good luck, and I'm sure you'll do great!

Another thing you could do is volunteer for team projects or committees. This gives you a natural reason to interact with different people. I remember when I joined the office social committee, it really helped me get to know my colleagues better.

One final suggestion is to use small talk as a starting point. Compliment someone on their work or ask for their opinion on something. People generally like to feel valued, and it can lead to more meaningful conversations.
Remember, making friends takes time, so don't be too hard on yourself. Just be genuine and patient, and you'll gradually build those connections.

tasks.title: Talking about a Personal Experience
prompt: Talk about a time when you spoke in front of a group of people. Maybe you can talk about a presentation you gave in class, a report you delivered at work, or a speech you made at a wedding. Where did it happen, what did you say, and how did it make you feel?

paragraphs: I remember this one time when I had to give a presentation at work, and it was quite the experience. It was during our annual team meeting, and I was tasked with presenting our department's quarterly results. The meeting took place in our company's main conference room, which was packed with about 50 people, including senior management.

I had prepared a detailed PowerPoint presentation, focusing on our key achievements, challenges, and future goals. I started by introducing our team's objectives, then moved on to the numbers, highlighting our successes and explaining the areas where we fell short. I also included some graphs and charts to make the data more digestible.

Honestly, I was pretty nervous at first. My heart was racing, and I could feel my palms getting sweaty. But as I got into the flow of the presentation, I started to relax. I made sure to maintain eye contact with the audience and speak clearly. I even managed to throw in a couple of jokes to lighten the mood, which got a few laughs.

By the end of it, I felt a huge sense of relief and accomplishment. The feedback I received was overwhelmingly positive, and it really boosted my confidence. It was a great reminder that stepping out of your comfort zone can lead to some pretty rewarding experiences.

I remember this one time when I had to give a presentation in my university class. It was for my marketing course, and we were supposed to present a new product idea to the class. I was pretty nervous at first, you know, because public speaking isn't really my thing. But I had prepared well, so I tried to focus on that.

The presentation was in our regular classroom, but the professor had arranged the seats in a semi-circle to make it more interactive. I started by introducing our product - it was a smart water bottle that tracks your hydration levels. I explained the features, the target market, and our marketing strategy. As I got into the flow, I started feeling more comfortable. I even managed to crack a couple of jokes, which got some laughs from the class.

By the end of it, I was actually enjoying myself! The professor gave me positive feedback, and some classmates complimented my presentation skills. It was a great confidence booster. That experience taught me that with proper preparation, I can overcome my fear of public speaking. It's something I'll definitely remember whenever I have to speak in front of a group again.

I remember when I had to give a presentation in my university class last year. It was about climate change and its impact on Canadian agriculture. I was really nervous at first, but I prepared well by researching and practicing my speech. When I stood in front of the class, I started by explaining how rising temperatures are affecting crop yields in the Prairies. Then, I discussed potential solutions like drought-resistant crops and sustainable farming practices. As I spoke, I noticed my classmates were really engaged, which made me feel more confident. By the end, I was actually enjoying myself! The professor gave me positive feedback, and some students even asked follow-up questions. It was a great experience that taught me the value of thorough preparation and helped me overcome my fear of public speaking.

I remember when I had to give a presentation in my college class. It was about climate change, and I was really nervous. The room was full of students, maybe about 30 people. I started by explaining what climate change is and how it affects our planet. Then, I talked about some solutions we can all do to help, like recycling and using less plastic. My voice was shaking at first, but as I kept talking, I felt more confident. When I finished, everyone clapped, and my teacher said I did a good job. It made me feel proud and happy that I could share important information with others.

I remember when I had to give a presentation in my high school class. It was about Canadian history, and I was really nervous. The classroom was full, with about 30 students watching me. I talked about the War of 1812 and how it shaped Canada's identity. My voice was shaking at first, but as I continued, I started to feel more confident. I used some pictures and maps to make it more interesting. When I finished, my classmates clapped, and my teacher said I did a good job. It made me feel proud and more comfortable speaking in front of people. That experience helped me a lot in university when I had to do more presentations.

But I took a deep breath and started talking. I spoke about the First Nations people and how they lived before Europeans came. I also talked about the fur trade and how it changed Canada. As I continued, I felt more comfortable. My classmates were listening carefully and some were even taking notes. When I finished, my teacher said I did a good job. I felt proud of myself. It was a good experience for me. It helped me become more confident in speaking in front of others.

paragraphs: Well, I can certainly understand your friend's dilemma, eh? It's not easy to balance a fantastic career opportunity with the comfort of staying close to loved ones. But let me tell you, as a true Canuck, I think there's a lot to consider here.

First off, let's talk about the career benefits. This job overseas could be a real game-changer for her resume. It's like scoring a hat trick in the career hockey game, if you know what I mean. She'd gain international experience, which is as valuable as a loonie these days in our globalized economy. Plus, she'd be expanding her professional network faster than you can say 'double-double'.

Now, onto personal growth. Living abroad is an adventure that'll make her grow faster than a Manitoba wheat field in summer. She'll learn about new cultures, maybe pick up a new language, and gain a perspective on life that you just can't get staying in the Great White North. It's the kind of experience that'll shape her worldview and make her appreciate our Canadian multiculturalism even more.

But I get it, leaving friends and family behind is tougher than a Canadian winter without a toque. However, with today's technology, staying connected is easier than ever. She can schedule regular video calls, share her adventures on social media, and maybe even convince some friends to visit. Before she knows it, she'll be back for a visit, bringing stories and souvenirs like maple syrup to a pancake breakfast.

So, here's my advice: encourage her to weigh the pros and cons, but remind her that opportunities like this don't come along every day. It might be scary, but sometimes you've got to leave the comfort of your igloo to see what the world has to offer. Whatever she decides, make sure she knows you'll support her, whether she's here or on the other side of the world.

tasks.title: Expressing Opinions
prompt: Do you think that mature students, those returning to university after time in the workforce, should get the same special discounts on travel, entertainment, and products as younger students? Explain your reasons.

paragraphs: I strongly believe that mature students should receive the same special discounts as younger students, and here's why.

First off, returning to university after years in the workforce is a significant financial commitment. Many mature students have family responsibilities and mortgages to pay, making their financial situation often more challenging than that of younger students. These discounts could make a real difference in their ability to pursue education without undue financial stress.

Secondly, mature students bring valuable life experience to the classroom, enriching the learning environment for everyone. By offering them discounts, we're acknowledging their unique contribution to the academic community. It's a way of saying, 'We value your experience and want to support your educational journey.'

Lastly, from a societal perspective, encouraging lifelong learning benefits us all. When mature students upgrade their skills or change careers, they contribute more effectively to the economy. These discounts could be seen as an investment in our collective future, fostering a culture of continuous learning and adaptation in our rapidly changing world.
In conclusion, providing equal discounts to mature students isn't just fair - it's a smart move that benefits individuals, educational institutions, and society as a whole.
I believe mature students should absolutely receive the same discounts as younger students, and here's why.

First off, returning to school as an adult often comes with significant financial challenges. Many mature students are balancing tuition costs with supporting families or paying mortgages. These discounts can make a real difference in their ability to afford education. For example, a friend of mine who went back to school at 35 found that the transportation discount was crucial for her to attend classes while still managing her household budget.

Secondly, mature students contribute just as much to the academic community as younger students. They bring valuable life experience and often enhance classroom discussions. By offering them the same benefits, we're recognizing their important role in the educational system. I've seen this firsthand in my university classes, where mature students often provide practical insights that complement the theoretical knowledge.

Finally, education should be accessible to everyone, regardless of age. These discounts aren't just about saving money - they're about creating equal opportunities for lifelong learning. When we support mature students, we're investing in a more educated and skilled workforce, which benefits everyone in the long run.

In conclusion, mature students face unique challenges and make valuable contributions. Extending the same discounts to them is not only fair but also beneficial for our educational institutions and society as a whole.
I believe mature students should definitely get the same discounts as younger students. Here's why.

First, mature students often face more financial pressures. They might have families to support or mortgages to pay. These discounts can really help them manage their budgets better. For example, a discount on public transportation could save them hundreds of dollars each semester.

Second, mature students contribute a lot to the university community. They bring work experience and different perspectives to class discussions. Giving them discounts is a way to recognize their value. It's like saying 'we appreciate what you bring to our school.'

Finally, education should be accessible to everyone, regardless of age. Discounts help make that possible. If we want more people to keep learning throughout their lives, we need to support them. These small savings can make a big difference in someone's decision to return to school.
In conclusion, mature students deserve these discounts just as much as younger ones. It's fair, it's practical, and it supports lifelong learning.

I think mature students should get the same discounts as younger students. First, they are students too, so they should have the same benefits. Second, many mature students have financial problems because they have families to support. Discounts can help them save money. For example, my friend John went back to school at 35. He has two kids and his wife doesn't work. The discounts really help him.

Another reason is that mature students often have more expenses. They might need to pay for childcare or transportation. Discounts can make it easier for them to study. For instance, my cousin Sarah is a mature student. She uses student discounts for bus tickets and it saves her a lot of money.

Finally, giving discounts to mature students is fair. They are working hard to improve their lives, just like younger students. They should have the same opportunities. In conclusion, I believe mature students deserve the same discounts as younger students because they face similar challenges and need support too.

I think mature students should get the same discounts as younger students. First, they are students too. They pay the same fees and study the same things. It's not fair to treat them differently just because they are older.
Second, many mature students have families to support. They often have less money than younger students. Discounts can help them save money for important things like food and rent.

Finally, mature students bring good experience to the classroom. They share what they learned at work. This helps everyone learn more. Giving them discounts is a way to say thank you for their contribution.
In conclusion, mature students work hard and face challenges. They deserve the same help as younger students. Discounts can make their lives a little easier.

tasks.title: Describing an Unusual Situation
prompt: You are at a shoe store and you see a pair of interesting shoes that your sister, Josie, might like. Call Josie and describe in detail what the shoes look like. Ask her if she would like to buy them.

paragraphs: Hi Josie, I'm at the shoe store right now and I've spotted something that I think you'd absolutely love! There's this unique shoe sculpture that's the centerpiece of the display. It's placed on a striking red pedestal, which really makes it stand out. The design is intricate and artistic, definitely something that catches your eye immediately.

Around the sculpture, there are several other shoes scattered throughout the scene. Some are on the ground, while others are placed on various surfaces. It feels like a creative exhibition of footwear, each piece adding to the overall artistic vibe of the display.
I think these shoes would be perfect for you, especially if you're into unique and artistic designs. What do you think? Should I grab them for you, or do you want to come and check them out yourself?

Hi Josie, I'm at the shoe store and I just saw a pair of shoes that I think you'd really like. They're quite unique-they're actually a sculpture of a shoe, placed on a red table that really makes them stand out. The colors are vibrant, with a mix of purple and green that gives them a really artistic look. The design is intricate, with lots of details that make them look like a piece of art rather than just regular shoes.

In the background, there are some books scattered around, which adds to the whole artistic vibe of the scene. It's like they've created a little reading nook with the shoes as the centerpiece. I can't stop looking at them-they're so different from anything I've seen before.
What do you think? Would you like me to get them for you? I think they'd be a great addition to your collection, especially if you're into unique, statement pieces. Let me know!

Hi Josie, I'm at the shoe store and I just saw a pair of shoes that I think you'd really like. They're on a red table in the center of the display. The shoes are a deep navy blue with gold accents, and they have this unique pattern that looks like waves. The material seems to be a mix of leather and suede, giving them a really classy yet modern look. What caught my eye is the sole - it's a bright yellow, which adds a fun pop of color. They're definitely eye-catching but still elegant enough for work or a night out. There are also two books in the display, one near the top right and another at the bottom right, which makes the whole setup look really artistic. I think these would be perfect for you, especially with your style. Would you like me to get them for you? They seem to be in your size.

Hi Josie, I'm at the shoe store and I found something you might like. There's this really unique shoe sculpture here. It's on a red table, so it really stands out. The design is super artistic and detailed. Around it, there are some books scattered on the table and even a few on the floor. In the background, there's a handbag and a clock, which adds to the whole scene. It's like a mix of art and everyday items. I think it's really cool and thought you might like it too. What do you think? Should I get it for you?
